sections.title: What are Stacks?
sections.content:
A **stack** is a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure. The last element you push onto the stack is the first element you get back when you pop. The physical analogy is a stack of plates: you add to the top and remove from the top. You never access the plate at the bottom without removing everything above it first.

Real-world examples of LIFO semantics are everywhere. Your browser's back button is a stack of visited URLs - the most recently visited page is the first one you go back to. Undo in a text editor is a stack of operations. The CPU's function call stack is literally named after this data structure: each function call pushes a frame, each return pops one. When a recursive function calls itself too many times, it overflows this stack.

In JavaScript, we implement stacks using arrays. `arr.push(x)` adds to the top (end) in O(1). `arr.pop()` removes from the top in O(1). `arr[arr.length - 1]` peeks at the top without removing. Never use `arr.shift()` or `arr.unshift()` for stack operations - those operate on the front and are O(n).

The key intuition for when to use a stack: whenever you need to **remember previous states to process the current element**, and the most recently stored state is the most relevant one. If you're processing an element and need to look back at 'the last thing I saw', a stack holds that last thing at its top.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: The strongest signal for a stack is any problem involving matching or nesting: brackets, HTML tags, function calls, or any structure where an opening token must be matched with the most recent unmatched closing token. The second signal is 'next greater/smaller element' - whenever you need to find, for each element, the first element to its right that is larger (or smaller), a monotonic stack gives O(n).
signals: next greater or next smaller element
previous greater or previous smaller element
evaluate an arithmetic or postfix expression
maintain order while processing: most recent unmatched

Bracket Matching
Monotonic Stack
Core Template
sections.explanation: Bracket matching: push on open, check and pop on close, empty stack at end means all brackets closed. Monotonic stack: iterate forward, pop when the current element violates the decreasing order (meaning it IS the next greater for popped elements), push index (not value) so you can record answers by position.

items.name: Monotonic Decreasing Stack
items.description: For 'previous greater element' or 'next smaller element', flip the condition. Maintain an increasing stack (pop when current is smaller) for next-smaller, or iterate backward with a decreasing stack for previous-greater. The amortized O(n) argument holds for all variants.

items.name: Stack with O(1) Min/Max
items.description: Augment each stack entry with the minimum (or maximum) of all elements at or below it. Store pairs `[value, currentMin]`. When you push, `currentMin = Math.min(value, stack.top.min)`. Pop discards the pair. This gives O(1) `getMin()` with O(1) push/pop.

items.name: Two Stacks as a Queue
items.description: Use an 'inbox' stack for enqueue and an 'outbox' stack for dequeue. When the outbox is empty, pour the entire inbox into it (reversing order). Each element is moved at most once, giving amortized O(1) per operation. This is the implementation principle behind efficient FIFO queues.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n) for all stack-based linear scans
sections.space: O(n) worst case for the stack
sections.explanation: In bracket matching, each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once - O(n). In the monotonic stack, each element is pushed and popped at most once across the entire iteration - O(n) total, even though the inner `while` loop looks like it could be expensive. The stack holds at most n elements at any time, giving O(n) space.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Popping from an empty stack without checking: `stack.pop()` on an empty array returns `undefined` silently in JS without throwing an error. In bracket matching, if a closing bracket arrives and the stack is empty, that's an immediate `false` - check `stack.length > 0` before every pop.

Forgetting that the stack must be empty at the end of bracket matching: unclosed brackets remain in the stack after the loop. `return stack.length === 0` is the correct final check. Returning `true` after the loop exits without this check accepts `'((('` as valid.

Monotonic stack direction confusion: for 'next greater element', use a decreasing stack and pop when current element is GREATER than top. For 'next smaller element', use an increasing stack and pop when current is SMALLER. Getting the direction backwards produces next-smaller results when next-greater is needed.

Treating a stack as FIFO: stacks process in LIFO order. If you need the first-inserted element to come out first (e.g., for level-order traversal), you need a queue, not a stack. Using a stack for BFS produces DFS traversal order, which will give wrong answers on shortest-path problems.

Using `arr.shift()` for dequeue to simulate a queue with a stack: `shift` is O(n) because it shifts all elements. For queue-like behavior, use an actual queue (pointer-based dequeue) or the two-stacks-as-queue pattern.

items.title: Trapping Rain Water
items.why: Can be solved with a monotonic stack - tests ability to recognize when a popped element's answer depends on the new top and the current element.

items.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
items.why: The hardest pure monotonic stack problem - uses previous-smaller and next-smaller indices to compute the maximum-area rectangle for each bar.

items.title: Daily Temperatures
items.why: Direct next-greater-element problem on temperatures - tests the monotonic decreasing stack template and index-based result recording.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Queues are the FIFO counterpart to stacks - while stacks give you the most recent item, queues give you the oldest item, which is the property needed for BFS level-order traversal and shortest-path algorithms.
